a: Thomas Edison developed the phonograph, which recorded on tinfoil-wrapped cylinders, in 1877; its patent issued February 19, 1878. Emile Berliner patented the flat-disc gramophone on November 8, 1887.

q: What is the difference between a phonograph and a gramophone?
a: Edison's phonograph (1877) recorded on cylinders, first tinfoil and later wax. Berliner's gramophone (1887) used flat discs with spiral grooves, which were far cheaper to mass-produce, and the disc won: Edison switched to discs in 1913.

Columbia launched the 33 1/3 rpm LP in June 1948, and RCA Victor answered with the 7-inch 45 rpm single in January 1949. After the war of the speeds, both companies issued both formats by 1950: the LP became the album and the 45 the single.

q: What were 78 rpm records made of?
a: Shellac resin mixed with fillers such as clay, slate or limestone, plus carbon black and cotton fibers. They were made commercially from 1897 to the late 1950s, and the era had no fixed standard for speed or equalization.

It is the standard equalization curve, approved January 29, 1954, that cuts bass and boosts treble when a record is made; a phono preamp reverses it on playback. Before it, labels used different curves.

q: When did stereo records come out?
a: The RIAA adopted the Westrex 45/45 single-groove stereo system as the US standard on December 27, 1957. Audio Fidelity offered a stereo demo disc by mail that December.

q: When did vinyl hit its low point?
a: In the US, RIAA LP and EP shipments fell to about 900,000 in 2006; SoundScan's consumer count bottomed at 857,000 vinyl albums in 2005. In the UK, just over 200,000 LPs were bought in 2007.

In the US, vinyl passed CDs by revenue in 2020 and by units in 2022; in 2025 it sold 46.8 million units against 29.5 million CDs (RIAA). In the UK vinyl passed CD by value in 2022, but in 2024 CDs still led by units, 10.5 million to 6.7 million (BPI).
